title: Tropical Storm Lala Leaves 200,000 Without Power and 100 Homes Damaged Across Hawaii
excerpt: The storm, which briefly reached Category 1 hurricane strength, is pulling away from the islands after battering the Big Island, Maui, and Oahu with flooding, mudslides, and wind gusts.
body:
• More than 200,000 utility customers remain without power across Hawaii as Tropical Storm Lala pulls away from the island chain, with nearly 70% of the Big Island still dark.
  • At least 100 homes were damaged or destroyed, and one person died in a storm-related car accident, according to Governor Josh Green.
  • Airports in Hilo and Kona were closed Saturday and are expected to reopen Sunday, while flash flood warnings remain in effect for Oahu and the Big Island.
  • Lala could regain hurricane strength by midweek as it moves westward through the Central Pacific.

From Hurricane to Tropical Storm — But the Damage Is Done

Tropical Storm Lala weakened below hurricane strength Sunday morning after brushing Hawaii's Big Island as a Category 1 storm with 75 mph sustained winds. The downgrade offered little comfort to the more than 200,000 utility customers across the island chain who woke up without electricity, or to the residents of at least 100 homes that Governor Josh Green said were "damaged and lost" during a Sunday news conference.

https://x.com/GuntherEagleman/status/2088933780924817695

The storm's eyewall came within 30 miles of the Big Island's southern tip Saturday evening, close enough to deliver hurricane-force gusts across Hawaii, Honolulu, and Maui counties. The mountainous terrain amplified winds at higher elevations, snapping power poles and downing transmission lines across a 42-mile span on the Hamakua Coast.

"Several occupied homes may have been swept off their foundations, and based on that, civil defense has initiated a search and rescue mission."

— Kimo Alameda, Hawaii County Mayor

Flooding Overwhelms Roads and Triggers Rescues

The Big Island bore the brunt of Lala's impact. The National Hurricane Center reported up to 30 to 35 inches of total rainfall since the storm began lashing Hawaii late Friday — enough to trigger a "Particularly Dangerous Situation" flash flood warning, a rare designation reserved for the most extreme flood events. Video released by the Hawaii Department of Transportation showed floodwaters overtaking roads, and rescuers pulled occupants from a vehicle stuck in rising water Saturday night.

Oahu, including Honolulu, came under flash flood warnings Sunday morning as Lala's outer rainbands swept across the state capital. Hawaiian Electric warned that repair crews were hampered by hurricane-force winds, rain, and downed trees blocking access to damaged infrastructure.

Both Hilo International Airport and Ellison Onizuka Kona International Airport were closed Saturday, with officials expecting them to reopen Sunday. Travelers were advised to check with airlines before heading to terminals.

One Death Reported; Search Operations Continue

One person was killed in a storm-related car accident Saturday evening, Governor Green confirmed. At a separate news conference, Hawaii County Mayor Kimo Alameda said there were no other confirmed storm deaths, though search and rescue operations were continuing in areas where homes had been swept from foundations.

"It appears that no one died beyond the one car accident, which we're not sure if it was completely connected to the storm or not," Green said. "But if you're out driving around in a storm with winds and rain like that, turn around, go home because it's dangerous."

Storm Exits But Risks Remain

Lala is tracking west-northwest away from the islands and is expected to fully exit the Hawaiian chain by 8 a.m. local time Monday. Tropical storm warnings remain in effect for Kauai, Oahu, Molokai, Lanai, and Maui. Heavy rainfall is becoming more sporadic across most islands, but Kauai is still being grazed by Lala's core.

Forecasters warn of continued flooding and mudslide risks as saturated ground gives way under additional rain. The storm could regain hurricane strength by Tuesday or Wednesday as it moves farther into the Central Pacific over warmer waters.

Emergency crews have begun damage assessments and recovery efforts, though widespread outages, fallen trees, and debris on roadways are slowing access. More than 250,000 customers were without power at peak, and Hawaiian Electric has warned that restoration could take days in the hardest-hit areas.

What to Watch

The Federal Emergency Management Agency is monitoring the situation. Governor Green has activated the National Guard and requested federal disaster assistance. For Hawaii's Indian community and NRI travelers with plans to visit the islands, the state advises checking airline and hotel status before departure and avoiding all non-essential travel to affected areas through midweek.
